parts.title: The statement and the last step
parts.line: What is proved, and the final move
parts.summary: The five theorems in Mathlib’s terms, and how “no zeros to the right of the line” becomes “all zeros on it”.
story: `Statements.lean` writes the hypotheses in Mathlib’s own terms. `Main.lean` derives all five headline theorems from one result, `grh`: no Dirichlet L-function vanishes to the right of Re s = 1/2.

The last move is mirror symmetry (`New/Main`, `Lib/Analytic/ZeroSymmetry`). Zeros come in pairs reflected across the line, so a zero off the line would have a twin to its right, and `grh` forbids that.

parts.title: From a bound to the zeros
parts.line: A one-sided bound on primes rules out zeros
parts.summary: A weighted count of primes whose error “sees” the zeros, and why bounding that error from above is enough.
story: `Zeros/PrimeError` defines a weighted prime count and its remainder R_q. Its transform has poles exactly at zeros of L-functions, so the zeros show up as waves in the count of primes.

`Zeros/Criterion` turns a bound into a zero-free region. An eventual bound from above, R_q(x) ≤ A·x^(β−1), excludes zeros to the right of β. No lower bound is needed. Its notes cite Landau (1905) and Suzuki (2024).
`OneSidedBound` proves the bound with β = 1/2 + ε, using the main inequality (part 4) and the prime number theorem at a far-out second cut-off (`Zeros/PrimeNumberTheorem`), and ends with `grh`.

parts.title: The setup
parts.line: The data, the scales and the yardsticks
parts.summary: The number field, the scales x, x₁, b and m, the prime sums being compared, and the heights and lattices used to measure.
story: `Data` fixes everything the argument works with: a number field E built from ℚ(√−d) and roots of unity, its places, the level, the twists, and the scales. The GUIDE’s size table puts the number of lifts m between √x and 2√x.

`PrimeSums` defines the main amount and the remainder, the prime sums that the main inequality compares. `Lattices` provides heights over all places, twisted lattices, index and covolume: the yardsticks used to measure a family of forms from above and below.
Nearly every other part uses these files.

parts.title: The three theorems and the main inequality
parts.summary: Theorems A and B bound a family of forms from above, Theorem C from below; the main amount cancels and a bound on primes is left.
story: `ShortAndEnough` states Theorem A (a multiple of the projected Poincaré series has short lifts and small index) and Theorem B (a few translates span almost all of the target forms). Theorem C, the lower bound, is in part 7.

`MainInequality` puts them together. Up to errors, main amount ≤ (V + 2δ)/dim ≤ main amount − (n/dim)·m·remainder. The main amount cancels, which leaves an upper bound on the remainder of the prime sum. That is the bound part 2 needs.

parts.title: Theorem A: the composite lift
parts.line: A chain of about √x theta lifts, highly divisible
parts.summary: Theta lifts chained m times, derivatives that count primes, the seesaw identity: short lifts with small index.
story: `UpperBound` builds the chain. Source forms are lifted m times between definite hermitian spaces X₀ → X_m and restricted to Y_m: the composite lift. Its `Objects` folder defines the main objects, which much of the rest of the proof also uses. The seesaw identity (`Seesaw/SeesawIdentity`) says the lower chain applied to Poincaré series is a constant times the composite lift.

`Derivatives` supplies the divisibility: jets (Taylor coefficients) of theta functions are divisible by primes in a controlled way. The GUIDE calls them “derivatives that count primes”, and `Sharpness` shows the bound is attained. A nonzero number can’t have more prime factors than its size, so guaranteed divisibility becomes an upper bound on a sum over primes: Stepanov’s 1969 idea, done with whole numbers.
`UpperBound/Divisibility` and `UpperBound/Size` then show the composite lift is highly divisible and not too big. That is Theorem A.

parts.title: Theorem B: enough forms
parts.line: A second moment shows a few translates span
parts.summary: A Petersson-type second moment, with Bessel functions and unfolding, shows a few translates span almost all target forms.
story: `Spanning` proves Theorem B with a second-moment argument: the moments (`SecondMoment`), equal multiplicities (`Multiplicities`), measures and Bessel functions (`Bessel`), unfolding (`Unfolding`), a main term and the remaining terms.
Its conclusion is that a few translates of the normalised Poincaré map span almost all of the target forms.

parts.title: Theorem C: the lower bound
parts.summary: Determinants, one lift at a time, and congruences: covolume and twice the index are at least about the main amount.
story: Theorem C (`Determinant/Twist/LongForms`) says that covolume plus twice the index is at least about the main amount: integral forms are long.

`Determinant` picks a twist for each prime, computes norms of theta lifts and of whole chains, and uses an exchange identity of Siegel–Weil type. `OneLift` studies a single lift: its volume and height, Hecke L-values as squared norms, their valuations, and “false lifts”.

`Congruences` controls denominators. It uses Galois representations, anticyclotomic twists with small Selmer groups, the local loss, and lifting crystalline classes. `Appendix` supplies discrete series with a large gap.

ideas.title: Waves
ideas.line: The primes are made of waves
ideas.text: The count of primes is a smooth curve plus one wave per zero of zeta. The hypothesis says every wave grows like √x and no faster.

ideas.title: A ceiling
ideas.line: A bound from above is enough
ideas.text: To rule out zeros to the right of the line, an upper bound on a weighted prime sum is enough. No lower bound is needed.

ideas.title: Multiplicity
ideas.text: A nonzero number can’t have more prime factors than its size. Derivatives of theta functions give numbers whose divisibility by primes is guaranteed.

ideas.title: The chain
ideas.text: Each lift adds a layer of divisibility, and each has a price. The number of lifts, between √x and 2√x, balances them at the square root.
